plain_english: I've been thinking for a long time, my friend Serenus, about how to describe your state of mind. The best comparison I can find is this: You're like someone who has recovered from a long, serious illness. They still feel occasional aches and twitches. Even though they've beaten the disease completely, they still worry it might come back. They're perfectly healthy, but they keep checking their pulse with the doctor. Whenever they feel a little warm, they panic that the fever is returning. These people aren't sick, Serenus — they're just not used to being well. It's like a calm sea that still has small ripples after a storm has passed. What you need isn't the harsh medicine I mentioned earlier. You don't need to hold yourself back, get angry with yourself, or scold yourself harshly. What you need is the last thing on the list: confidence in yourself. Believe that you're on the right path. Don't let yourself be pulled away by all the wandering tracks that cross your path from every direction. Some of these false paths even circle around the right one.
original_excerpt: I have long been silently asking myself, my friend Serenus, to what I should liken such a condition of mind, and I find that nothing more closely resembles it than the conduct of those who, after having recovered from a long and serious illness, occasionally experience slight touches and twinges, and, although they have passed through the final stages of the disease, yet have suspicions that it has not left them, and though in perfect health yet hold out their pulse to be felt by the physician, and whenever they feel warm suspect that the fever is returning. Such men, Serenus, are not unhealthy, but they are not accustomed to being healthy; just as even a quiet sea or lake nevertheless displays a certain amount of ripple when its waters are subsiding after a storm. What you need, therefore, is, not any of those harsher remedies to which allusion has been made, not that you should in some cases check yourself, in others be angry with yourself, in others sternly reproach yourself, but that you should adopt that which comes last in the list, have confidence in yourself, and believe that you are proceeding on the right path, without being led aside by the numerous divergent tracks of wanderers which cross it in every direction, some of them circling about the right path itself.

plain_english: What you want — to live without constant worry — is a great thing. In fact, it's the greatest thing of all. It almost makes you like a god. The Greeks call this steady calmness of mind _euthymia_. Democritus wrote an excellent book about it. I call it peace of mind. There's no need to translate Greek words exactly — what matters is finding a name that captures the same meaning, even if it takes a different form. So what are we looking for? A mind that always stays on a steady, calm course. A mind that's pleased with itself and takes pleasure in what's around it. A mind that feels this joy without interruption and stays peaceful — never getting too high or too low. This is "peace of mind." Now let's think about how to achieve it in general terms. Then you can take whatever parts of this universal cure work for your own situation.
original_excerpt: What you desire, to be undisturbed, is a great thing, nay, the greatest thing of all, and one which raises a man almost to the level of a god. The Greeks call this calm steadiness of mind _euthymia_, and Democritus's treatise upon it is excellently written: I call it peace of mind: for there is no necessity for translating so exactly as to copy the words of the Greek idiom: the essential point is to mark the matter under discussion by a name which ought to have the same meaning as its Greek name, though perhaps not the same form. What we are seeking, then, is how the mind may always pursue a steady, unruffled course, may be pleased with itself, and look with pleasure upon its surroundings, and experience no interruption of this joy, but abide in a peaceful condition without being ever either elated or depressed: this will be "peace of mind." Let us now consider in a general way how it may be attained: then you may apply as much as you choose of the universal remedy to your own case.

plain_english:
We need to drag this whole disease into the light. Then each person will see their own piece of it. At the same time, you'll realize how much less you suffer from putting yourself down than those people who are trapped by some flashy promise they made. They're crushed by some grand title or honor. Shame — not their own choice — forces them to keep up the act.

The same thing applies to people who suffer from being wishy-washy and constantly changing their minds. They always love most what they just gave up. And it applies to those who just yawn and waste time. Add to these the people who are like bad sleepers — they toss and turn, trying one position and then another, until they finally find rest through pure exhaustion. When forming their life habits, they often end up adopting some that they don't stick with because they hate change, but because old age caught them living that way, and old age is slow to change. Add also those who aren't fickle at all, but who have their dullness to thank for that — not their consistency. They go on living not the way they want to, but the way they started living.

There are countless other special forms of this disease. But it has only one effect: making people dissatisfied with themselves.
original_excerpt: Meanwhile we must drag to light the entire disease, and then each one will recognize his own part of it: at the same time you will understand how much less you suffer by your self-depreciation than those who are bound by some showy declaration which they have made, and are oppressed by some grand title of honour, so that shame rather than their own free will forces them to keep up the pretence. The same thing applies both to those who suffer from fickleness and continual changes of purpose, who always are fondest of what they have given up, and those who merely yawn and dawdle: add to these those who, like bad sleepers, turn from side to side, and settle themselves first in one manner and then in another, until at last they find rest through sheer weariness: in forming the habits of their lives they often end by adopting some to which they are not kept by any dislike of change, but in the practice of which old age, which is slow to alter, has caught them living: add also those who are by no means fickle, yet who must thank their dulness, not their consistency for being so, and who go on living not in the way they wish, but in the way they have begun to live. There are other special forms of this disease without number, but it has but one effect, that of making people dissatisfied with themselves.

plain_english: This comes from an unhealthy mind and desires that people are afraid to express or can't fulfill. These people either don't dare try for what they want, or they fail and live entirely on hope. Such people are always restless and changing — which is inevitable when you live in suspense. They'll try any path to get what they want. They teach themselves to use both shameful and difficult methods. When their hard work fails, they're crushed by the disgrace of failure. But they don't regret wanting the wrong things — they regret wanting them uselessly. Then they start feeling sorry for what they've done and afraid to try again. Their mind gradually falls into endless back-and-forth, because they can neither control their passions nor give in to them. They hesitate because their life can't develop properly. They decay as disappointments make their mind numb.
original_excerpt: This arises from a distemperature of mind and from desires which one is afraid to express or unable to fulfil, when men either dare not attempt as much as they wish to do, or fail in their efforts and depend entirely upon hope: such people are always fickle and changeable, which is a necessary consequence of living in a state of suspense: they take any way to arrive at their ends, and teach and force themselves to use both dishonourable and difficult means to do so, so that when their toil has been in vain they are made wretched by the disgrace of failure, and do not regret having longed for what was wrong, but having longed for it in vain. They then begin to feel sorry for what they have done, and afraid to begin again, and their mind falls by degrees into a state of endless vacillation, because they can neither command nor obey their passions, of hesitation, because their life cannot properly develope itself, and of decay, as the mind becomes stupefied by disappointments.

plain_english: All these problems get worse when people hate hard work so much that they retreat into idleness and private studies. But this is unbearable for minds that crave public life, want action, and are naturally restless. Such minds don't have enough inner resources to sustain themselves. When they lose the entertainment that busy work provides, they can't stand being home, alone, or within four walls. They start to dislike themselves when left with only themselves for company. This creates that terrible restlessness and self-hatred, that constant mental fidgeting that can never find peace, that miserable and reluctant endurance of forced leisure. When people are too ashamed to admit what's really bothering them, and when pride makes them bottle up their pain, all those trapped desires choke each other in that cramped space with no outlet. This leads to depression and despair, and countless waverings of an unsteady mind that hangs in suspense with unfulfilled hopes and gets crushed by disappointed ones. This explains the mental state of people who hate their own idleness, complain they have nothing to do, and watch others' progress with bitter jealousy. Miserable laziness breeds envy, and people who can't succeed themselves want everyone else to fail too.
original_excerpt: All these symptoms become aggravated when their dislike of a laborious misery has driven them to idleness and to secret studies, which are unendurable to a mind eager to take part in public affairs, desirous of action and naturally restless, because, of course, it finds too few resources within itself: when therefore it loses the amusement which business itself affords to busy men, it cannot endure home, loneliness, or the walls of a room, and regards itself with dislike when left to itself. Hence arises that weariness and dissatisfaction with oneself, that tossing to and fro of a mind which can nowhere find rest, that unhappy and unwilling endurance of enforced leisure. In all cases where one feels ashamed to confess the real cause of one's suffering, and where modesty leads one to drive one's sufferings inward, the desires pent up in a little space without any vent choke one another. Hence comes melancholy and drooping of spirit, and a thousand waverings of the unsteadfast mind, which is held in suspense by unfulfilled hopes, and saddened by disappointed ones: hence comes the state of mind of those who loathe their idleness, complain that they have nothing to do, and view the progress of others with the bitterest jealousy: for an unhappy sloth favours the growth of envy, and men who cannot succeed themselves wish every one else to be ruined.

plain_english: When we resent other people's success and give up on our own, we become angry at fate. We complain about the times we live in. We hide in corners and brood over our misery until we're sick of ourselves. The human mind is naturally restless and eager to move. It loves any chance to get excited and forget itself. The worse someone's character, the more they enjoy this. They like to exhaust themselves with constant activity, just like infected wounds that crave the hands that hurt them and enjoy being touched. A foul itch loves anything that scratches it. In the same way, I promise you, minds that are eaten up by desires like cancerous sores actually enjoy hard work and troubles. Some things please our body while also causing pain — like tossing and turning before you're even tired, or constantly shifting positions to cool off. It's like Homer's Achilles, lying first on his face, then on his back, arranging himself in different positions. Like sick people do, he can't stand any position for long and treats constant movement like medicine.
original_excerpt: This dislike of other men's progress and despair of one's own produces a mind angered against fortune, addicted to complaining of the age in which it lives, to retiring into corners and brooding over its misery, until it becomes sick and weary of itself: for the human mind is naturally nimble and apt at movement: it delights in every opportunity of excitement and forgetfulness of itself, and the worse a man's disposition the more he delights in this, because he likes to wear himself out with busy action, just as some sores long for the hands that injure them and delight in being touched, and the foul itch enjoys anything that scratches it. Similarly I assure you that these minds, over which desires have spread like evil ulcers, take pleasure in toils and troubles, for there are some things which please our body while at the same time they give it a certain amount of pain, such as turning oneself over and changing one's side before it is wearied, or cooling oneself in one position after another. It is like Homer's Achilles, lying first upon its face, then upon its back, placing itself in various attitudes, and, as sick people are wont, enduring none of them for long, and using changes as though they were remedies.

plain_english: So people wander around aimlessly. They travel to distant shores. Sometimes they go by sea, sometimes by land. They try to calm that restless nature that's never happy with where it is. "Let's go to Campania now. I'm tired of all this fancy countryside. Let's see some wild places. Let's hike through the mountains of Bruttium and Lucania. But even in this wilderness, I want something beautiful to look at. My eyes are tired of all this rough landscape. Let's go to Tarentum with its famous harbor, mild winters, and rich lands that once fed huge armies. Now let's go back to the city. I miss the shouting and noise. It would be fun to watch some gladiator fights too." So one trip follows another. One sight gets swapped for the next. As Lucretius said, "Every person flees from himself." But what good does it do? You can't escape yourself. You follow yourself everywhere. You drag yourself along like your own worst burden.
original_excerpt: Hence men undertake aimless wanderings, travel along distant shores, and at one time at sea, at another by land, try to soothe that fickleness of disposition which always is dissatisfied with the present. "Now let us make for Campania: now I am sick of rich cultivation: let us see wild regions, let us thread the passes of Bruttii and Lucania: yet amid this wilderness one wants something of beauty to relieve our pampered eyes after so long dwelling on savage wastes: let us seek Tarentum with its famous harbour, its mild winter climate, and its district, rich enough to support even the great hordes of ancient times. Let us now return to town: our ears have too long missed its shouts and noise: it would be pleasant also to enjoy the sight of human bloodshed." Thus one journey succeeds another, and one sight is changed for another. As Lucretius says:— "Thus every mortal from himself doth flee;" but what does he gain by so doing if he does not escape from himself? he follows himself and weighs himself down by his own most burdensome companionship.

plain_english: We need to understand that our problems aren't caused by where we are — they're caused by who we are. We're weak when we have to endure anything. We can't handle work or pleasure for very long. We can't stick with our own projects or other people's projects. This weakness has driven some people to kill themselves. They kept changing their minds about what they wanted, but they always ended up in the same place. They left themselves no room for anything new. They got sick of life and sick of the world itself. When all pleasures stopped being fun, they started asking themselves: "How long do we have to keep doing the same thing?"
original_excerpt: We must understand, therefore, that what we suffer from is not the fault of the places but of ourselves: we are weak when there is anything to be endured, and cannot support either labour or pleasure, either one's own business or any one else's for long. This has driven some men to death, because by frequently altering their purpose they were always brought back to the same point, and had left themselves no room for anything new. They had become sick of life and of the world itself, and as all indulgences palled upon them they began to ask themselves the question, "How long are we to go on doing the same thing?"
